newsitem.title: USA: Weak Swiss economy boosts dollar vs Swiss franc.
newsitem.headline: Weak Swiss economy boosts dollar vs Swiss franc.

text.p: The dollar rose against the Swiss franc, which slumped to its lowest level in nearly two years on Wednesday as Switzerland's economy showed more signs of distress.

The Swiss franc also fell to a 41-month low against the German mark, on speculation that Swiss interest rates, already among the world's lowest, are still stifling the economy and must be lowered again.

Demonstrating that two years of sub-par economic growth has taken a heavy toll, a report from semi-official credit watchdog Schweitzerischer Verband Creditreform on Wednesday said business bankruptcies in Switzerland rose 9.6 percent in the first 11 months of 1996, compared to last year.

"I think it is part and parcel of what's been weakening the Swiss (franc)," said David Gilmore, partner at consulting firm Foreign Exchange Analytics. "You also have a central bank that has condoned depreciaton and is committed to low interest rates."
The dollar climbed to 1.3340 Swiss francs, its highest since early January 1995, before settling late Wednesday at 1.3295 Swiss, up from 1.3260 late Tuesday.
The economy should benefit from a weaker franc, which would help Swiss exporters by making their products cheaper in other countries, analysts said.

This year, the Swiss National Bank has loosened the credit reins agressively, after raising interest rates every quarter for almost two years. With rates lower than every major currency except the yen, the Swiss franc has been shunned by investors looking for higher yields.

The dollar also rose to a high of 1.5552 marks, closing at 1.5517, up from 1.5500 late Tuesday. But the dollar's gains were dampened by the German currency's strength against the struggling Swiss franc.

In contrast to its strength versus the Swiss franc, the mark fell against the British pound, indirectly boosting the dollar, on expectations that German interest rates will eventually fall while British deposit rates might soon become Traders said the Bundesbank will probably keep rates steady at its bi-weekly meeting on Thursday after German M3 money supply growth -- the central bank's favourite barometer of inflation -- slowed notably in November.
M3 expansion slowed to an annual rate of 8.0 percent in November, below October's 8.4 percent growth rate.

While slower money supply growth should please the Bundesbank, M3 is still above the central bank's 4.0 to 7.0 percent target and most traders expect it is still too worried about inflation to ease credit yet.

"But you never know," said Ben Strauss, assistant vice president at Bank Julius Baer & Co. "Most of their rate moves catch the market by surprise, as opposed to the (Federal Reserve), where most of their rate moves are well anticipated."
The pound rose to $1.6747 from $1.6707 late Tuesday on news that the number of unemployed Britons fell almost 96,000 in November.
"It seems to be pointing the way towards higher rates in the U.K., probably next year," said Dennis Pettit, foriegn exchange manager at Long-Term Credit Bank of Japan.
The dollar fell to 113.69 yen from 113.87 yen, but rose to Canadian $1.3667 from C$1.3636.
